title: CADC
text:
What did they say?

  


COLD OPEN.
Say nothing for the first ten seconds; the field drifts, far away, hundreds of them. Click 1: a slow zoom to a dozen you can read. These are real: tweets from the week 2 corpus, restaurant and film reviews from the labs, two lines from State of the Union addresses. Click 2: labels fly in and attach, slowly at first, then faster than anyone can read. That is what a machine does, and the speed is what the room should notice. Click 3: the camera pushes in on one of them. “862 patients test positive” was labelled positive, because something saw the word and stopped reading. Let the room notice before you say anything, then ask the two questions yourself: how do we get a machine to do this at all, and how would we know when it is wrong? Both come back on the dark slide after the first two figures.

title: CADC
section: The world went digital in about twenty years
text:
The world went digital in about twenty years

  


Hilbert, M., & López, P. (2011). The world’s technological capacity to store, communicate, and compute information. Science, 332(6025), 60–65. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1200970
International Data Corporation. (2024). Global DataSphere and StorageSphere forecasts. IDC. — post-2007 storage.
Epoch AI. (2026). Global AI computing capacity is doubling every 7 months. https://epoch.ai/data-insights/ai-chip-production — AI panel.


The labels need glossing out loud, since none of them are self-explanatory:
Optimally compressed exabytes. They did not count devices or files; they converted everything to the number of bits it would take to store the same content under ideal compression. That is the only way a vinyl record, a VHS tape and a hard disk end up on one axis. One exabyte = a billion gigabytes.
Analog vs digital. Analog is paper, film, vinyl, cassette, VHS. Note the shape: analog capacity does not just lose share, it peaks around 2000 and then shrinks in absolute terms. The blue overtakes it around 2002. The paper itself says only “the early 2000s”; 2002 is what interpolating 25% in 2000 to 94% in 2007 gives, hence the ≈ on the marker. Recent enough that most of the room was alive for it.
General-purpose computing. Machines that can be programmed to do anything: PCs, servers, phones, calculators. Hilbert & López separate these from application-specific computing, the fixed-function chips in a washing machine or a DVD player, which they measured separately and which was much larger in aggregate. Measured in instructions per second, so the axis is log: each gridline is a hundredfold.
Why the compute line is straight. On a log axis a straight line is exponential growth, with a constant doubling time; it looks tame only because the axis is log. If a student asks whether growth slowed: single-thread CPU performance did collapse after Dennard scaling ended around 2005, but aggregate world capacity is core counts times device counts times datacentres, and that kept compounding. AI-specific compute went the other way entirely, doubling every 6–9 months since 2020, far steeper than this line.
The AI line. This one comes from Epoch AI (2026), not Hilbert & López: total AI chip capacity growing ~3.3× a year since 2022, a doubling every 7 months, about 5.2 million operational H100-equivalents by end of 2025. Note that the two right-hand series are in different units: general-purpose is instructions per second, AI accelerators are 8-bit floating-point operations. They share an axis so you can compare shape and order of magnitude, but you cannot read a like-for-like ratio off it. Say that if anyone asks.
The rates. 58% a year for general-purpose computing 1986–2007 is theirs. Carrying that same rate past 2007 is an assumption, and you should say so. Same for the storage figure after 2007: ~12 zettabytes installed by 2025 is an IDC industry estimate. Nobody has repeated their exact inventory since.
Ask before clicking: “how much bigger do you think it gets?” Then click. The 2007 total becomes a sliver you can barely see, which is what the second half of the animation is for.

title: CADC
section: Much of what we know about human behavior
text:
Much of what we know about human behavior


  
    ... is based on what people tell us 
    
      
        
        Self-report measures in surveys
      
      
        
        Responses in experimental research
      
      
        
        Accounts in qualitative interviews
      
    
    Useful for measuring motivations, attitudes, or feelings, but such measures can be biased:
    reported and actual behaviour diverge systematically.
  

  
    ... not based on records of actual behavior
    
      messagespostscommentsreviewsnews articleswiki entriestranscriptsparliamentary debatescode
    
    Communication that was never explicitly elicited for
    research, but is stored and available at scale. How can we use it?
  



Parry, D. A., Davidson, B. I., Sewall, C. J. R., Fisher, J. T., Mieczkowski, H., & Quintana, D. S. (2021). A systematic review and meta-analysis of discrepancies between logged and self-reported digital media use. Nature Human Behaviour, 5(11), 1535–1547. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-021-01117-5
Scharkow, M. (2016). The accuracy of self-reported internet use — A validation study using client log data. Communication Methods and Measures, 10(1), 13–27. https://doi.org/10.1080/19312458.2015.1118446


The left column. Ask how they have measured media use so far; almost every answer is one of these three. That is the discipline’s default, and for good reason: an attitude or a motive is not lying around to be picked up, so you have to ask.
The bias claim. Parry et al. (2021) meta-analysed 106 comparisons of logged versus self-reported digital media use: the association is only about r = .38, and self-reports are mostly over-estimates. The error also correlates with what we study: heavy users misreport differently from light users. Scharkow (2016) found the same with client log data. So the bias has a direction, and averaging will not remove it. If someone objects that self-reports are still fine for attitudes, agree; that is the boundary.
The right column. These are old phenomena that now leave a record. Debates were always spoken, but are now transcribed; complaints always existed, but are now reviews with a timestamp.
Do not oversell it. Someone will point out this record is skewed: not everyone posts, platforms shape what is said, APIs decide what you can see. Agree, and say we return to it in the lab: digital traces have their own validity problem, different from that of self-report and no smaller.
Bridge. The obvious objection: it is text, and you cannot run a regression on a tweet. That is the next slide.

title: CADC
section: An ordinary question, too many articles
text:
An ordinary question, too many articles



How did Dutch news cover the housing crisis between 2015 and 2025?

Did the coverage get more negative over the decade?
Did the framing shift from economics to fairness?
Whose voices were quoted: politicians, developers, tenants?

Nothing computational about the question itself: this is the content analysis communication research has been doing since the 1950s
To answer it you would read every article mentioning woningmarkt in four national outlets, 2015 to 2025



  Articles to code100,000
  Minutes to read and code one× 4
  
  Hours≈ 6,700
  Working days≈ 830
  3 years
  one coder, full time, no holidays, reading each article exactly once



Do the arithmetic out loud, slowly. This is the only big number in the deck, and it is there to make “just read them” visibly impossible rather than merely tedious.
Ask what they would do instead. Two answers come up, and both deserve taking seriously:
“Sample it.” A real answer, and it costs you the thing you wanted: the whole decade, and the rare cases. A sample of 500 is perfectly defensible for average tone and useless for “how often were tenants quoted”, because the interesting cases are rare.
“Get more coders.” Also real, also expensive, and it buys a new problem: two coders do not agree with each other. That problem has a name and a number attached, and they meet it in week 2.
Bridge: so either you give up the decade, or you find something that can read 100,000 articles.

title: CADC
section: The two big questions this course will answer
text:
The two big questions this course will answer

How can we analyse all of this text — automatically?
How can we make sure that the analysis is valid?


Say both out loud and say that the second one is the harder of the two. Week 1 is about the first; week 2 turns to the second, and the course stays with it from then on.

title: CADC
text:
Objectives and learning goals


After completion of the course, you will…

identify the data-analytic problem in a communication question, state it precisely enough for a machine, and judge whether a computational method can answer it
describe the text-classification pipeline end to end and name where each decision can go wrong
explain what each method costs and assumes, from word counts to large language models, and when the cheap one is right
treat measurement as a research question and decide when a number is not good enough to publish
run a small text-analysis study in a group, from research question to presentation


Only the third names methods. The others outlast whatever tool is current when you graduate.



  



Read the goals as the exam blueprint, because that is what they are: the exam asks you to frame a problem, to locate a decision in the pipeline, and to judge whether a measurement can be believed. It does not ask you to write code from scratch.
The diagram is the familiar text-mining Venn, rebuilt for this course. It has six steps: one circle arrives per click, and on the last step the middle is labelled “This course” where the original Venn has a field. Worth saying that nobody arrives holding all four circles: you each bring one or two, and the course works where all four overlap.

title: CADC
text:
Skills and methods
With regard to the specific methods taught in R, you will be able to…

import and wrangle text into a tidy table, and turn it into tokens, counts and embeddings
apply dictionaries, supervised classifiers, word embeddings and LLMs to the same texts
build a gold standard, compute coder agreement (Cohen’s κ, Krippendorff’s α), read a confusion matrix, and report precision, recall and F1
obtain data for a project of your own from APIs, archives and existing corpora
make an analysis reproducible from a clean start, document its decisions, and disclose what an AI tool did


Each of these is practised in the labs, the homework or the group project.


Worth saying plainly: nobody is expected to arrive knowing R. The course website has a “Before the first lab” page that walks through the installs and ends with a small setup check; anyone whose laptop cannot run RStudio messages us on Canvas before the first lab.

section: An example: a surprising source of information
text:
An example: a surprising source of information



2009, Rwanda: a survey of 1,000 customers of the largest mobile provider (demographics, assets, wealth)
The researchers also had the call records of 1.5 million subscribers
A model trained on the 1,000 predicts wealth from calling behaviour for everyone else
Location comes free: the towers that carried the calls




Predicted wealth by district, and by cell tower in the inset. Blumenstock, Cadamuro & On (2015), Science.



Blumenstock, J., Cadamuro, G., & On, R. (2015). Predicting poverty and wealth from mobile phone metadata. Science, 350(6264), 1073–1076. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4420


Stop after the second bullet and ask: so far, is this traditional social science? Yes: a survey with a random sample. The computational part is the third bullet: the survey becomes training data. Most of this course has that shape: a small, carefully measured set, scaled up by a model.

title: CADC
text:
Computational social science

Social science that uses algorithmic tools and large, unstructured data to study human and social behaviour
Complements surveys, experiments and interviews rather than replacing them; the question comes first
The usual ingredients

Digital traces: posts, logs, transactions, call records
Automated text, image, or video analysis
Machine learning for classification and prediction
Simulation of social processes



Different data, the same questions.


Lazer, D., Pentland, A., Adamic, L., Aral, S., Barabási, A.-L., Brewer, D., … Van Alstyne, M. (2009). Computational social science. Science, 323(5915), 721–723. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1167742

title: CADC
text:
Why now?



Big data: social media, digital archives, digitised newspapers, logs of almost everything
Constant records: traces of people and organisations accumulate as a by-product of ordinary life
More compute: powerful, cheap, and available without owning a computer
Sophisticated tools: text classification, topic models, word embeddings, and now large language models, much of it open source


The first figure of this lecture showed three of these developments.

title: CADC
section: Big data · three things that help
text:
Big data · three things that help







Characteristic
In one line




1 · Big
Rare events, heterogeneity, small differences become studyable


2 · Always on
Continuous collection: unexpected events, real time


3 · Non-reactive
Being measured does not change the behaviour




None of the three guarantees that the data are good.


Salganik, M. J. (2018). Bit by bit: Social research in the digital age. Princeton University Press. Chapter 2.3.

title: CADC
section: Big data · seven things that get in the way
text:
Big data · seven things that get in the way







Characteristic
In one line




4 · Incomplete
Made for another purpose; your variable is missing


5 · Inaccessible
Held by companies and governments


6 · Non-representative
Users of a platform are not a population


7 · Drifting
The system changes under you


8 · Algorithmically confounded
Behaviour is shaped by the platform’s engineering


9 · Dirty
Spam, bots, duplicates, junk


10 · Sensitive
Some of it should never have been collected




Salganik, M. J. (2018). Bit by bit: Social research in the digital age. Princeton University Press. Chapter 2.3.


Two to dwell on because they come back in every project: incomplete (a browser log tells you every URL and nothing about why) and algorithmically confounded (what people see on a feed is what a ranking system chose to show them, so the behaviour you observe is partly the platform’s).

title: CADC
section: What computational methods buy, and what they cost
text:
What computational methods buy, and what they cost



Opportunities


Actual behaviour instead of reports of it
People in their own context, not a lab
Very large N, and therefore statistical power
Patterns that were not observable before



Pitfalls


The techniques are demanding
The data are often proprietary and cannot be shared
Samples are biased in ways that are hard to see
Little metadata; unknown provenance
Models we no longer understand

title: CADC
text:
Computational communication science

“The emerging subfield that investigates the use of computational algorithms to gather and analyze big and often semi- or unstructured data sets to develop and test communication science theories.”
van Atteveldt & Peng (2018)


Large and complex data sets
Consisting of digital traces and other naturally occurring data
Requiring algorithmic solutions to analyse
Used to develop and test communication theory


Van Atteveldt, W., & Peng, T.-Q. (2018). When communication meets computation: Opportunities, challenges, and pitfalls in computational communication science. Communication Methods and Measures, 12(2–3), 81–92. https://doi.org/10.1080/19312458.2018.1458084

title: CADC
text:
Where it shows up

Political communication: polarisation, hate speech, campaign messaging, parliamentary debate
Journalism: coverage across decades, framing, gender representation
Social media use: logged rather than reported use; the spread of information and emotion
Health communication: what health information circulates, and where


Three studies, three kinds of data: news text, television, and (for the ethics part) a social network.

title: CADC
section: Example 1 · Seventy years of nuclear news
text:
Example 1 · Seventy years of nuclear news



51,528 New York Times stories on nuclear technology, 1945–2014
Far too many for human coding
A topic model finds recurring clusters of words and tracks them over time
Research → Cold War → accidents → proliferation




Attention to four topics over time. Jacobi, van Atteveldt & Welbers (2016).



Jacobi, C., van Atteveldt, W., & Welbers, K. (2016). Quantitative analysis of large amounts of journalistic texts using topic modelling. Digital Journalism, 4(1), 89–106. https://doi.org/10.1080/21670811.2015.1093271

title: CADC
section: Example 2 · Who is on German television?
text:
Example 2 · Who is on German television?



Six channels, 72 sample days, every frame between 08:00 and 24:00
A face detector finds and crops every face; a second network estimates gender and age
16 million faces: nobody can watch this much television, but a validated classifier can
The classifier is checked against hand-coded faces first; without that step the numbers mean nothing




Detect, crop, classify, validate: the four steps for text, with pixels as input.



Jürgens, P., Meltzer, C. E., & Scharkow, M. (2022). Age and gender representation on German TV: A longitudinal computational analysis. Computational Communication Research, 4(1), 173–207.


This sits next to the news study to show that the pipeline also works beyond text. Detect and crop is obtain, the cropped face is represent, the age/gender network is classify, and the hand-coded check is validate. Say that now: the pipeline slide only comes in part III, and this is the evidence that it generalises.

title: CADC
section: Example 2 · And the answer is the same everywhere
text:
Example 2 · And the answer is the same everywhere



6.3 million of the 16 million faces were female, a proportion of .39 (95% CI .37 to .42)
The imbalance holds across news, sport and advertising, hour by hour and day by day
It is also stable over time, so the pattern is structural
Women on screen are also, on average, younger than men








Each tile is one hour of one day. Left: share of female faces. Right: estimated age.



Jürgens, P., Meltzer, C. E., & Scharkow, M. (2022). Age and gender representation on German TV: A longitudinal computational analysis. Computational Communication Research, 4(1), 173–207.


Let them look at the left panel for a moment before saying anything. The green wash is the finding, and it is more convincing than the point estimate.
Two things worth drawing out. First, the CI: .37 to .42 is narrow because n is 16 million, and the width of that interval is a measurement question, not a substantive one. Second, the flatness: if the bias were driven by one genre or one time of day you would see stripes. You do not, and that is what makes it structural.
If someone asks how the classifier knows gender: it does not. It predicts a binary label from pixels, it was trained on labelled photographs, and it is wrong some of the time in ways that are not evenly distributed. That is exactly why the validation step exists, and week 2 is about how you would report it.

title: CADC
text:
What is a text?






Hieroglyphs carved into a temple wall







A printed journal article







The HTML behind a web page






All three are symbols in a sequence, meaningless on their own
Meaning arrives only when someone interprets them, in context
Automated text analysis tries to bridge that gap


Krippendorff, K. (2018). Content analysis: An introduction to its methodology (4th ed.). SAGE.


Ask which of the three is text. All of them, and the hieroglyphs make the point hardest, because for 1,400 years nobody could read them. The symbols never changed; what was missing was the interpretation. That is Krippendorff’s definition in one image: content analysis makes “replicable and valid inferences from texts to the contexts of their use”, and the context is doing the work.
The HTML panel is worth a second: most text you will ever obtain arrives wrapped in markup like this, and stripping it is part of step 01 of the pipeline, planned from the start. That is Thursday’s lab.

title: CADC
text:
From text to numbers

  

PLAYGROUNDTokeniser sandbox

A teaser: each of the three shapes gets its own week, so do not teach them here. Six clicks. Stop on the document–term matrix and ask what got lost (the order of the words). The Playground’s tokeniser sandbox is where they change this matrix with their own hands before Thursday. The next three slides do the middle step properly, because the later weeks build on it.

From tokens to counts


library(tidytext)

  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>     # one row per token
  count(doc, word)                 # one row per document and word

Three tiny texts, so every number can be checked by eye
unnest_tokens splits, lowercases and drops punctuation in one call; count does the arithmetic

title: CADC
text:
The document–term matrix


texts |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  count(doc, word) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = word,
              values_from = n,
              values_fill = 0)     # a word absent from a text counts 0

The same counts, turned on their side: one row per document, one column per term, a count in every cell
Compare it with the survey table four slides ago: rows are cases, columns are variables. Text has become ordinary data
Most cells are zero, and with real corpora almost all of them are. The matrix is sparse

The matrix keeps which words occur and how often; it drops the order they came in. This is the bag-of-words assumption

title: CADC
text:
Where the numbers come from








Level of language
It organises
This course uses it in




Morphology
how words are formed
tokens, stems, n-grams (weeks 1 to 3)


Syntax
how sentences are built
word order, mostly thrown away until week 3


Semantics
what words and sentences mean
word embeddings (week 3)


Pragmatics
how language is used in context
language models (week 4)




Every method in this course is a decision about which of these levels to keep.


Hvitfeldt, E., & Silge, J. (2021). Supervised machine learning for text analysis in R. CRC Press. Chapter 1.

title: CADC
text:
Content analysis, by hand

Choose the texts
Define the units and the categories
Write a codebook: rules another coder could follow
Code, which is where the time goes
Check agreement between coders, revise the rules, code again
Analyse frequencies, relationships, change over time


Steps 1, 2, 3 and 5 remain when a machine does step 4, and that is the pipeline.


This is the bridge to Part III. Automated content analysis is the same method, with a machine in step 4 and a much larger step 5.

title: CADC
text:
The pipeline

  


Six clicks. The goal is always the same: put a label on texts that do not have one. The last click is the syllabus: weeks 2, 3 and 4 change only what feeds step 03. This figure returns in every lecture; the site’s navigation is built from it.

title: CADC
text:
01 · Obtain

Public data sets: parliamentary records, news corpora, research archives; ideal when they exist
Scraping: websites and archives you collect yourself; trivial or very hard depending on the site, and always a legal question
Third parties: APIs, commercial archives, data donations; custom formats, rate limits, terms of use that change


Obtaining text is rarely the interesting part and often the slowest. Plan for it.

title: CADC
text:
02 · Represent

Create features: break text into units (words, n-grams, sentences)
Transform: lowercase, strip punctuation, remove stopwords, stem
Select: drop very rare and very frequent terms
Build the data: the document–term matrix from Part II for counting and classic learning; dense vectors for neural models


Every item on this list is a decision, and every decision changes the measurement. Modern models leave you fewer, but some remain.

Rule-based
Unsupervised
Supervised
Pre-trained models




Logic
“if word X occurs, the text means Y”
“these words cluster; I decide what the cluster means”
“texts like these were labelled Y, so this one is probably Y too”
“given everything I have read, this text is Y”


Meaning comes from
the researcher, in advance

a sentiment dictionary

title: CADC
text:
04 · Validate

Every classifier is a black box to some degree, dictionaries included, and manual coding too
The machine does not understand the text; it predicts a label from features, and it is wrong some of the time
So the analysis must be shown to be valid: compare its labels with a known good
The reference is usually a gold standard: a subset coded by trained humans, with agreement checked


A number becomes a measurement only once it has been validated.

title: CADC
section: The pipeline runs on problems, not on questions
text:
The pipeline runs on problems, not on questions

  


This is the hinge of the lecture, and the reason the course is called computational analysis rather than automated analysis. Six clicks.
Everything so far has been machinery: four steps, in order, the same every week. But the pipeline cannot start until somebody has turned a question into something it can consume, and that move takes judgement. It is the skill this course is trying to teach.
Do not rush step 4. The moment where two of the three cards dim is the one students remember: a method does not tell you which texts to gather or what to compare them against. Those are decisions you make and then have to defend in writing, and no amount of accuracy rescues a bad one.
If someone objects that the machine could decide the other two as well, good: it could suggest them, but it cannot justify them, and the homework asks for the justification.
Land on the last caption and go straight into the next slide: getting that judgement onto paper is exactly what a specification is.

title: CADC
text:
A computational problem, stated properly

Input: what exactly goes in? One article, one sentence, one post? Whose?
Output: what exactly comes out? A label, a score, a number per month?
Success criterion: what would count as good enough, decided before you run anything
Failure check: how would you find out that you were wrong?


Most labs include a sketch like this, on paper, before you touch a tool.


Most labs have a “sketch first” step built on these four lines, on paper, before any code. Say so now: the framing comes before the code, every week.

title: CADC
text:
The same question, framed twice



Not yet a problem


“Is the housing coverage negative?”
Negative to whom, measured how, compared with what?



A problem you can run


Input: one article
Output: negative / neutral / positive
Criterion: agrees with a trained human coder
Check: on 100 articles nobody used to build it



The right-hand column is also precise enough for others to refute.

title: CADC
text:
Timeline of natural language processing

  


Six screens of four events, one click each; #N in the iframe URL opens screen N. Screens: foundations (Bayes, Lovelace, Boole, Turing) · the birth of the field (Shannon, Weaver, the Turing test, Chomsky) · symbolic NLP and the winters (perceptron, ELIZA/ALPAC/General Inquirer, knowledge-based NLP, backpropagation) · the statistical turn (1990s, LIWC/LDA, AlexNet, word2vec) · sequence models to scaling (seq2seq, Transformer, BERT/GPT, GPT-3) · language models (ChatGPT, 2023, multimodal, reasoning and agents). Each screen wears the era colour of the strip. No caption on the figure: narrate it.

title: CADC
text:
Same task, four generations

One measurement task runs through weeks 1 to 4
One hand-coded gold standard, built by you in week 2
Four methods scored against it: counting, a dictionary, a trained classifier, a language model


So by week 4 you can say which method is better, for this task, on this data, rather than which is newer.

title: CADC
text:
A controversial study

2012: Facebook alters the news feeds of 689,003 users for one week: fewer positive posts for some, fewer negative for others
Emotional words in the users’ own posts shift in the same direction; the effect is real and tiny
The users were not asked, informed or debriefed
Published in PNAS in 2014; the reaction was immediate


The terms of service made it legal; whether it was right is a separate question.


Kramer, A. D. I., Guillory, J. E., & Hancock, J. T. (2014). Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks. PNAS, 111(24), 8788–8790. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1320040111

title: CADC
text:
Ethical challenges

Privacy: personal data, data breaches, and the question of what you send to a company’s model
Bias: models inherit the biases of their training data, and validation is the only way to see it
Transparency: complex models are hard to explain, which makes them hard to hold to account
Manipulation: the same tools shape opinion and behaviour, with or without consent
Cost: energy for training and running models, and ownership of models and data


Van Atteveldt, W., & Peng, T.-Q. (2018). When communication meets computation. Communication Methods and Measures, 12(2–3), 81–92. https://doi.org/10.1080/19312458.2018.1458084

title: CADC
text:
Four principles

Respect for persons: treat people as autonomous; honour their wishes
Beneficence: understand and improve the risk–benefit profile of the study
Justice: risks and benefits should fall on the same people
Respect for law and public interest: privacy, copyright, access rights


The first three come from the Belmont Report (1978), the fourth from the Menlo Report (2012). Salganik applies all four to digital research.


Dittrich, D., & Kenneally, E. (2012). The Menlo Report: Ethical principles guiding information and communication technology research. U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
Salganik, M. J. (2018). Bit by bit: Social research in the digital age. Princeton University Press. Chapter 6.

title: CADC
text:
Principles for computational communication research







Principle
In practice




1 · Privacy and data security
Consent where you can; know where your data go


2 · Fairness
Look for bias in data and models; validate


3 · Transparency
Prefer interpretable models; share complex ones


4 · Care with experiments
Consent and debriefing, or assess the harm


5 · Environmental impact
Test small first; most tasks need no giant model


6 · Cross-cultural sensitivity
Models do not cross languages for free


7 · Engagement
Involve the communities your research touches

Assistant: it helps you write code or prose that you check yourself; disclosed

title: Your own study
text:
Part III · Weeks 6 to 8


Your own study

For three weeks you work in a group on one question you chose. Here you apply the methods to a study of your own: you find real data, measure something with it, show that the measurement is worth reporting, and defend the whole study in front of the class.


30% of the final grade, one grade per group: see Assessment. Dates and rooms are on Weeks.





THE THREE WEEKS


  6
  
    Kickoff · groups, question, data
    Get the data
    Monday's lecture puts the four weeks back together as one pipeline and
    covers which data you can obtain in 2026. Then you form groups, pick a
    question, and go and get data. The one hard rule of week 6: by Thursday you
    have the data in a file you can open. A plan to obtain it does not count.
    
      Due end of week 6: the data-access plan. One page: source, how you get it, legal basis, what you will have in hand, and your fallback if it falls over.
    
  



  7
  
    No lecture · supervision on Tuesday and Thursday
    Measure, then check the measurement
    You build the measurement, and then do the part that separates this from a
    data-journalism piece: hand-code a sample, compute agreement, and report how
    well your automated measure reproduces it. A project without a validation
    section cannot pass, however interesting the finding.
  



  8
  
    The mini conference
    Present your study
    A conference in miniature: a ten-minute talk per group plus five minutes of
    questions, and a poster gallery over the break. You present what you found,
    what you could not find out, and which number you would put in a paper. Both
    the talk and the poster need a validation section and are in English, and
    everyone attends the whole session: you are the audience too.
  




READING FOR WEEK 6




Article · read before Monday of week 6


Computational research in the post-API age
Why the data you can get for a project is no longer the data you could get ten years ago, and what that means for computational research. Read it together with this page, top to bottom.

Freelon, D. (2018). Computational research in the post-API age. Political Communication, 35(4), 665–668. https://doi.org/10.1080/10584609.2018.1477506

Read the article






GETTING DATA IN 2026


Getting the data is where many projects fail. The 2015 answer, “use the Twitter API”, no longer exists, and a group that spends two of its three weeks negotiating access has no project.



THE THREE-WEEK TEST

Before you commit to a source, answer three questions. If a source fails any of them, it will not work for a three-week project.

Can you download a sample today, without filing an application?
Is there a working R package or a documented endpoint, or are you writing a scraper from scratch?
If it breaks on Wednesday of week 7, what is your fallback?

The catch

Whatever the source, you still need a gold standard: a sample your group hand-coded itself. No project passes without one.




BEFORE YOU COLLECT ANYTHING



  
    Legal basis
    Is it personal data?
    A public post is still personal data under the GDPR. Ask what you are
    collecting, why that is the minimum you need, how long you keep it, and where
    it lives. Pseudonymise on import, not later.
  

  
    Ethics
    Does it need review?
    Anything involving participants (data donation, interviews, surveys)
    needs ethics approval before you start. Public, aggregate, non-sensitive text
    usually does not. If you are unsure, ask rather than guess.
  

  
    Hygiene
    What never goes in the repo
    API keys, tokens, raw personal data, and anything a participant gave you.
    Keys go in an environment variable; raw data stays local; the repo holds code
    and a script that fetches. This is graded.
  





WHAT A GOOD PROJECT LOOKS LIKE



Keep the question narrow
A well-measured claim about one construct in one corpus is better than a sweeping question answered badly. Three weeks is less time than it sounds, and week 8 is the conference, so you cannot use it as extra time.


Validate the measurement
Every group can get a language model to output labels. Your project should show what you did to find out whether those labels are any good, and what you found when you checked.


Report negative results
“The dictionary and the LLM disagree, and here is where and why” is a better project than a headline number nobody checked. You are not graded on the finding being exciting.


Name the limitations
Say what your study cannot show: how you sampled, what the data covers, which population your platform represents, and which classes your classifier never sees. Limitations you name precisely gain marks; leaving them out loses marks.





HOW IT IS GRADED










Criterion
What we look for
Weight




Question & framing
A communication question that a computational method can actually answer, stated precisely, with the construct defined before the tool is chosen
20%


Data & access
A defensible source, an honest account of what it covers and what it misses, sampling decisions made on purpose and documented
20%


Measurement & validation
A gold standard you built, agreement reported, the automated measure evaluated against it, and the right metric for the class balance you have
30%


Interpretation
Conclusions that match the evidence, limitations named precisely, and a clear statement of which number you would defend
20%


Presentation & poster
A clear ten-minute talk, a poster that is legible from two metres, and answers that hold up under questioning
10%





Draft rubric: the criteria are fixed, the weights may still move. One grade per group; individual adjustment only where a group reports a genuine imbalance to their supervisor before week 8. AI use follows the same rules as everywhere else: see AI use. Posters from previous cohorts will be linked here before week 6.

title: Tokeniser sandbox
text:
Playground

 Week 1 · Word frequencies


Tokeniser sandbox

Turning a pile of text into a table you can count takes a chain of small decisions. In this sandbox you make them yourself and watch the counts change.



What to do · 6 min

Read the default text, then tick remove stopwords and watch the ranking rebuild.
Try light stemming, then switch to bigrams.
Push the rare-word cutoff up until the table looks tidy, then read how many terms that deleted.



What you take away

Why the is usually the most frequent word, and what removing it costs.
That preprocessing is a chain of decisions, each one changing the number you would report.



Interactive: try the switches. Open full screen

What to notice

On the default text the tops the table at 3. Tick remove stopwords and the ranking changes completely: the “most frequent word” was an artefact of a choice.
Light stemming merges covers and coverage into one row. Convenient, and now you cannot tell them apart.
Switch to bigrams or trigrams: the vocabulary multiplies while nearly every count drops to 1. This is why n-gram models need far more data.
Drop terms appearing fewer than N times is standard practice for sparsity, and it silently deletes evidence. Watch the “N terms removed” line.

Used in Week 1 · Word frequencies.

title: Tidy wrangling
text:
02 REPRESENT Lab A · Tidy wrangling Week 1 · 105 min
Monday’s lecture made a simple point about computational communication science: before a computer can analyse anything, a text, a post or a log file has to become a table, with one row per case and one column per variable. This first lab makes you comfortable with that kind of table in R. You learn the five functions from the tidyverse that you will use in every lab of this course, filter(), select(), mutate(), group_by() and summarize(), and the pipe |> that chains them into a pipeline.
If you have never used R before, work through chapters 2–5 of R for Computational Social Science before the session. This lab assumes that you can open RStudio and run a line of code.

title: Tidy wrangling
text:
Part 1 · Political news in Europe

1 · Getting to know the data
We first load the tidyverse and then read the data with read_csv(). Because the file sits in the same folder as your script, the file name is enough.

library(tidyverse)

ess <- read_csv("ess-news.csv")
ess

R shows a tibble: the first ten rows, the number of rows and columns, and the type of every column (<dbl> is a number, <chr> is text). You can also click on ess in the Environment tab to browse the whole table.
These are the eight variables, taken from the ESS codebook:








Variable
Meaning
Values




id
respondent number



country
country code
e.g. NL, BE, DE


gender
gender
1 = male, 2 = female


age
age in years
999 = not available


news_min
minutes per day spent on news about politics
7777 = refused, 8888 = don’t know, 9999 = no answer


internet_min
minutes per day on the internet
6666 = does not use the internet, 7777–9999 = missing


pol_interest
interest in politics
1 = very … 4 = not at all; 7–9 = missing


trust_politicians
trust in politicians
0 = none … 10 = complete; 77–99 = missing



Keep this table open; you will need it later in the lab.


2 · Sketch the pipeline first


ON PAPER · ON YOUR OWN · 7 MIN


Do Dutch men and women differ in how much political news they follow?

Before you write any code, and without a laptop, answer these four questions, based on the four lines from the lecture.

Input: which rows and which columns do you need?
Output: what should the final table look like? How many rows, which columns?
Steps: in plain words, what has to happen between input and output?
Check: how would you notice if the answer were wrong?




3 · Rows and columns: filter() and select()
filter() keeps the rows that meet a condition. select() keeps the columns you name. In both, the first argument is the data and the rest says what to do with it.

nl <- filter(ess, country == "NL")
nl

select(nl, gender, news_min)

Note the double ==: a single = gives a value to an argument, a double == asks “is this equal?”. Other comparisons are != (not equal), >, <, >= and <=. You can combine conditions with a comma, which means and.
Exercise 1: Create a table young_nl with Dutch respondents under 30, and keep only the columns gender, age and news_min. How many rows do you expect? Write your guess down first.

# your code here



4 · Pipes
In Exercise 1 you probably stored an in-between result and used it again in the next line. This happens so often that R has a shortcut, the pipe |>. It takes the result on its left and puts it into the first argument of the function on its right. Read it as “and then”:

ess |>
  filter(country == "NL") |>
  select(gender, news_min)

This works because every tidyverse function takes a table and returns a table. From now on we will write most code as a pipe, with one step per line.


5 · New variables: mutate()
mutate() adds a column, or changes an existing one. Here we turn the gender codes into words, which will make every table and plot easier to read.

nl <- ess |>
  filter(country == "NL") |>
  mutate(gender = ifelse(gender == 1, "male", "female"))
nl

ifelse() takes a condition, the value if it is true, and the value if it is false.
Exercise 2: Add a column news_hours to nl that gives the political news use in hours instead of minutes.

# your code here



6 · Groups and summaries
group_by() splits a table into groups. summarize() then shrinks every group to a single row with the summary you ask for. n() counts the rows in a group.

nl |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            mean_news = mean(news_min))

Before you read the output: what do you expect? Men more, women more, or no difference?


THE TRAP

The code above runs without an error or a warning, and its answer is wrong. Find out why. Two hints: look at the codebook table again, and run summary(nl$news_min).

Exercise 3: Fix the summary so that it only uses real answers. Does the conclusion about men and women change?

title: Using AI in this course
text:
AI use · 2026


Using AI in this course

AI tools are everywhere, and we cannot realistically make you work without them. What we can do is hold you accountable for what you hand in. You may use AI for most of the work in this course, as long as you say how you used it, can account for everything you hand in, and can own the claims in it. This page explains the four categories of AI use and how to disclose them; the Assessment page explains how the grades are affected.





TWO LANES


We know from our own experience that the competence to use these tools well depends on knowledge you built without them. You cannot judge whether a classifier’s output is any good if you have never worked out what a confusion matrix means on your own. So the course runs two “lanes” on purpose, and always tells you which one you are in.




No AI


The exam and the check-ins
Supervised and closed: no tools, no model, no notes beyond what is allowed in the room. This is where we find out what you can do yourself (reading output, reading code, judging a design), which is the capability the other lane rests on.




AI permitted, but disclosed


Labs, homework and the project
In some parts of the weekly labs, in the homework and in the project, you may use whatever AI tools help you, as long as you disclose them as described below. Where a tool does the routine work, we ask for the judgement instead: why this decision, why this metric, what you rejected and why, and how you know the output is right. In week 4 you use AI as an instrument anyway, and you may also use it as an assistant or a thinking partner. You may not use it as a surrogate: you may not hand in work that was done solely by AI and that you therefore cannot defend without the output in front of you.






FOUR KINDS OF USE


We sort AI use into acceptable and unacceptable categories by what the tool did to the work, and therefore by what you have to be able to account for.






Category
What it means
What we ask of you




Instrument
The model performs a defined task whose output enters your work: classifying your texts, generating code you run, producing labels you analyse.
Method-level disclosure, written like a methods section: model and version, how the prompt was designed, and validation against your own judgement.


Assistant
Editing, grammar, translation, debugging, help searching. The intellectual content is yours; the tool touched the surface.
Which tool, for what, and what you did with its output: what you kept, what you changed, what you rejected.


Thinking partner
The model works on your own notes, drafts and materials, helping you stress-test ideas that are already yours.
Say what you discussed with it and what came out of it. You must be able to defend every claim without the output in front of you, and the text must be in your own voice.


Surrogate
The model produces the work and you put your name on it.
Not allowed. It falls under the VU fraud and plagiarism regulation, and no disclosure statement makes it acceptable.








HOW TO DISCLOSE



THE TEMPLATE

Every homework ends with a section C · AI disclosure. Write one block for each category you used, and say which parts you wrote without AI. For each use, answer four questions:

Which tool, and when (e.g. ChatGPT, 12 November; Claude in RStudio; GitHub Copilot)?
What for: which step or section, and what you asked it?
What you did with it: what you kept, what you changed, and at least one thing you rejected, with the reason.
How you checked it: how you know the code does what it says, or the claim is right.

If you used it substantially, paste your most important prompts in an appendix at the end of your file, or add a share link to the conversation.
The standard behind all of it: you must be able to reconstruct and defend the reasoning without the output in front of you. If you cannot, the category was Surrogate, whatever the disclosure says.




Example · light use


Only as an assistant
Assistant. ChatGPT (14 Nov), for one error message in step 4 (“object ‘word’ not found”). It explained that I had removed the column with select() two lines earlier. I fixed the order of the steps myself.
Not used for: the reflections, written without AI.




Example · medium use


Assistant and thinking partner
Assistant. Claude (20 Nov), to write the pivot_wider() call in step 6. I kept its code, checked the table against the confusion matrix by hand (the four cells add up to my 40 tweets), and rejected its suggestion to drop the neutral tweets, because my codebook defines neutral explicitly.
Thinking partner. After writing my error types in B2, I asked Claude whether it saw others. It suggested sarcasm; I checked tweets 12, 31 and 40 and it fits only 31, which I added as an example. The error types are mine.
Not used for: B1 and B3. Prompts in the appendix.




Example · homework 4


When the model is your method
Instrument. llama3.2:3b through Ollama, run on 19 Nov on my laptop, temperature 0, with a JSON schema. The prompt is my week 2 codebook, verbatim in step 2; all 40 replies are in my file. Validated against my gold standard (κ = .58, against .71 between my partner and me).
Assistant. ChatGPT (20 Nov), to turn my codebook into a prompt. It added an instruction to “be careful with sarcasm”, which I removed: it is not in my codebook, and the comparison with my partner’s coding would no longer be fair.
Not used for: the reflections.





NOT ENOUGH


AI use: ChatGPT was used for help with the code and to improve the text.

Which code? Which text? What did you keep, what did you change, what did you reject, and how did you check it? A disclosure like this counts as missing.

text:
MA Communication Science · Period 2 · 2026




Digital communication leaves more text behind than anyone can read: political messaging, news, social posts, support logs, open survey answers. This course is about turning that text into numbers so a computer can analyse it, and about finding out whether those numbers measure what you think they do.


New here? Start with Before the first lab (about an hour). How you are graded is on Assessment, what you may use AI for on AI use, and every date and room on Weeks. All rules in one document: the course manual (PDF).





WHAT YOU WILL LEARN

    Spot the data-analytic problem inside a communication question, state it
    precisely enough that a machine could attempt it, and judge whether a
    computational method can answer it at all.
  

  
    02
    
    Describe the text-classification pipeline end to end (obtain, represent,
    classify, validate) and name the point where each decision can go wrong. In
    R: import text, wrangle it into a tidy table, turn it into tokens, counts and
    embeddings.
  

  
    03
    
    Word counts, dictionaries, classic machine learning, word embeddings, large
    language models: what each costs and assumes, and when the cheapest one is
    good enough. In R: apply each of them to the same texts.
  

  
    04
    
    Build a gold standard, compute coder agreement, report precision, recall
    and F1 honestly, read a confusion matrix, and decide when a number is not good
    enough to publish.
  

  
    05
    
    Make an analysis reproducible from a clean start, document the decisions
    behind it, and disclose what a tool did and where your own judgement shaped
    the outcome.

    Develop a research question, run a small text-analysis study in a group,
    and present your findings to the room.
  





HOW A WEEK WORKS


Eight weeks in three parts: four weeks of methods, the exam in week 5, and three weeks on a project of your own. In the four weeks of methods, every week has the same rhythm.



Monday · lecture



Each week opens with a research problem and works toward a method that could solve it. The arc runs from counting words in the 1960s to prompting a language model today. Lectures are not mandatory, but the exam is built on them.

Say something. Labs run on discussion: about a coding decision, a metric, a result that looks too good.

text:
02 REPRESENT Lab B · Text wrangling & exploration Week 1 · 105 min
On Monday you saw how a text becomes numbers in three moves: split it into tokens, count them, and arrange the counts in a document–term matrix. Today you make those three moves yourself in R, first with the three sentences from the lecture, where you can check every number by eye, and then with more than two centuries of State of the Union speeches. Along the way you make your first plots with ggplot.
The package that does the text work is tidytext, which turns a text into a table with one row per word. From then on, everything you learned on Tuesday (filter(), mutate(), group_by(), summarize()) works on text too.

title: Text wrangling & exploration
text:
Part 1 · From text to numbers

1 · Three sentences, one matrix
These are the three sentences from the lecture. We store them in a small table with one row per document.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)

texts <- tibble(
  doc  = c("A", "B", "C"),
  text = c("The new law is good news.",
           "The new law is not good news.",
           "A disaster, this law."))
texts

unnest_tokens() splits the text into tokens. The first argument is the name of the new column (word), the second the column that holds the text. It also lowercases everything and removes punctuation.

tokens <- texts |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)
tokens

Now we count how often every word occurs in every document, and turn the result on its side with pivot_wider(): one row per document, one column per word. This is the document–term matrix from the lecture.

tokens |>
  count(doc, word) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = word, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

count(doc, word) is a shortcut for group_by(doc, word) |> summarize(n = n()). values_fill = 0 writes a 0 where a word does not occur in a document.
Exercise 1: Look at the matrix. Which two documents are most similar in their numbers? Do they mean the same? Write one sentence about what the matrix has thrown away.
Exercise 2: Tokenising is a decision. Check ?unnest_tokens and tokenise the three sentences into word pairs (bigrams) instead of single words. Which bigram would help you tell sentence A and B apart?

# your code here



2 · Sketch the pipeline first


ON PAPER · ON YOUR OWN · 5 MIN


What did Obama and Trump talk about in their State of the Union speeches?

This is the question for the rest of Part 1. Answer the four questions below without a laptop.

Input: which texts, and what is one document?
Output: what should the final table or plot look like?
Steps: what has to happen between input and output?
Check: how would you notice that the answer is misleading?




3 · The State of the Union corpus
The sotu package contains all State of the Union speeches from 1790 to 2020. The text and the information about each speech (president, year, party) are stored separately, so we first put them into one table.

library(sotu)

speeches <- as_tibble(sotu_meta) |>
  rename(doc_id = X) |>
  mutate(text = sotu_text)
speeches



4 · Tokens and counts

sotu_words <- speeches |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)
sotu_words

sotu_words |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

The information about each speech (president, year, party) rides along on every row, so you can group by president later.
Exercise 3: The most frequent words are the, of and and. Remove them with the stop-word list that comes with tidytext (stop_words) and anti_join(), and show the 20 most frequent remaining words. Before you run it: which words do you expect at the top?

# your code here



5 · Your first ggplot
A plot in ggplot is built from three parts, added with +: the data, the aesthetics (aes(): which column goes on which axis), and a geom (what to draw: bars, points, lines).

top_words <- clean_words |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(15)

ggplot(top_words, aes(x = reorder(word, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Number of times used",
       title = "The most frequent words in 240 State of the Union speeches") +
  theme_minimal()

reorder(word, n) sorts the bars by their count; coord_flip() turns the chart so that the words are readable.


6 · Obama and Trump

two_presidents <- clean_words |>
  filter(president %in% c("Barack Obama", "Donald Trump"))

two_presidents |>
  filter(word %in% c("america", "jobs", "applause")) |>
  count(president, word)



THE TRAP

From this table you might conclude that Obama talked much more about america than Trump did. That conclusion is not supported by the table. Why not? Count the speeches per president before you answer.

Exercise 4: Make the counts comparable. Compute, for each president, how often each word occurs per 1,000 words that president spoke (after stop-word removal). Then plot the ten most frequent words per president side by side. Tip: group_by(president) before a mutate() computes the total per president; slice_max(share, n = 10) keeps the top ten per group; facet_wrap(~president) draws one panel per president.

title: Before the first lab
text: Every lab runs on your own laptop, in R and RStudio. The first half of this page is a checklist to work through at home before Tuesday of week 1. The second half is a reference for the moments when the computer gets in the way instead of R: a download you cannot find, a zip that will not open, a file R says does not exist, a key you cannot type.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Before Tuesday of week 1


1



Two minutes


Check your laptop
A Windows laptop (Windows 10 or 11) or a Mac works. A Chromebook, an iPad, or a work laptop on which you are not allowed to install software will not run RStudio. If that is your situation, send us a message on Canvas before week 1 and we will find a solution together.





2



About twenty minutes


Install R, then RStudio
R is the program that runs your code. RStudio is the program you work in; it starts R for you. Both are free. Install R first.

WindowsmacOS



Go to cran.r-project.org, click Download R for Windows, then base, then the download link at the top.
Open the downloaded .exe file and click through, keeping every default. If Windows asks whether the app may make changes to your device, click Yes.
Go to posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop and download RStudio Desktop for Windows. Open it and keep every default.
Open RStudio from the Start menu: press Win, type RStudio, press Enter.




Check which chip your Mac has: the Apple menu (top left) > About This Mac. It says either Chip: Apple M… or Processor: … Intel.
Go to cran.r-project.org and click Download R for macOS. With an Apple chip, take the installer whose name ends in arm64.pkg; with Intel, the one ending in x86_64.pkg. The wrong one installs fine and then causes trouble later, so check twice.
Open the .pkg file and click through.
Go to posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop and download RStudio Desktop for macOS. Open the .dmg file and drag the RStudio icon into the Applications folder in that window. Then eject the RStudio disk in the Finder sidebar.
Open RStudio from Applications, or press Cmd + Space, type RStudio, press Enter. If macOS asks whether you are sure you want to open an app downloaded from the internet, click Open.




Done when the console (the pane at the bottom left) shows a line starting with R version 4., and typing 1 + 1 there and pressing Enter prints [1] 2.





3



Two minutes


Change three settings in RStudio
Open Tools > Global Options.

Under General, untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup, and set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never. Every session then starts empty, so your code has to work from top to bottom on its own, which is what happens when someone else runs it.
Under Code, tick Use native pipe operator, |>. The shortcut Ctrl + Shift + M (Cmd + Shift + M on a Mac) then types the pipe the labs use.

Click OK.





4



Ten to twenty minutes, on a good connection


Install the course packages
Packages add functions to R. This installs every package the labs use, so no lab has to start with a download. Copy the command (the button at the top right of the box does that) into the RStudio console and press Enter:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidytext", "sotu", "textstem",
                   "tidymodels", "textrecipes", "glmnet", "discrim",
                   "naivebayes", "LiblineaR", "stopwords", "tidyllm",
                   "rmarkdown"))
A lot of red text scrolls past. That is normal: R prints its progress in red. It is finished when the > prompt is back at the bottom of the console.
If R asks Do you want to install from sources the packages which need compilation?, type no and press Enter. If it asks whether to use a personal library, answer yes both times. What these questions mean.





5



Five minutes · this is also a rehearsal of every lab


Make a course folder and run the setup check
Make one folder for the course, for example cadc inside Documents. Every lab comes as a zip file, and every zip gets extracted into this folder.

Download the setup check (button below) and extract it into your course folder. On Windows: right-click the zip > Extract All. On a Mac: double-click it, then move the folder that appears into your course folder. More on zip files.
In the extracted folder, open setup-check.qmd in RStudio. If a double-click opens it in another program, use File > Open File in RStudio instead.
Click the green ▶ at the top right of the grey code box.

The check looks at your R version, your packages and the folder you are working in, and says [ok], [note] or [fix] for each. A [fix] line also says what to do. Done when nothing says [fix], and clicking Render at the top of the editor opens a web page with the same report.
If you get stuck, bring the check’s output to the first lab, or paste it into your message when you ask for help. It tells us most of what we need to know.
Download the setup check





6



A few hours, spread over the week before


Meet the console before the first lab
Work through chapters 2 to 5 of R for Computational Social Science. It runs in the browser, so this step works even before step 2. The first lab assumes you can open RStudio and run a line of code.
Open r4css





7



Five minutes


Can you do these ten things?
In the first labs, most time is lost on things around R: a file in the wrong folder, a zip that was never extracted, or a key nobody can find. If you hesitate on any of these, read the section it links to.

Find a file you just downloaded, without searching the whole computer. (Downloads)
Extract a zip file into a folder you chose. (Zip files)
See whether a file ends in .csv, .qmd or .zip. (File extensions)
Say which folder your course files are in, and whether it syncs to the cloud. (Where your files live)
Copy the full path of a file. (Paths)
Explain why read_csv("data.csv") works in one place and not in another. (R and your folders)
Run one code chunk of a .qmd file, then one single line. (RStudio in five minutes)
Type |, ~, {, [ and " on your own keyboard. (Keyboard)
Switch from your browser to RStudio without the mouse, and take a screenshot of part of the screen. (Keyboard)
Stop R when it seems stuck, and tell what a + in the console means. (When something goes wrong)

title: Before the first lab
text:
Downloads
Your browser saves files to the Downloads folder unless you told it otherwise. To find the file you just downloaded, click the download icon (an arrow) at the top right of the browser, then Show in folder (Windows) or the magnifying glass (Mac). On Windows, Ctrl + J opens that list in most browsers.

Downloading the same file twice gives week01-lab-a (1).zip. Delete the old one, or you will not know which one you extracted.
Downloads is a place files pass through. Do not work in it: move what you need into your course folder.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Zip files
A zip file packs several files into one, so a lab can be one download. Before you can use the files, they have to be extracted.

WindowsmacOS


Double-clicking a zip shows what is inside, but extracts nothing. Code you open from there cannot find its data, and whatever you save is lost (the explainer under Paths shows why). Instead:

Right-click the zip > Extract All…
Click Browse and choose your course folder, then Extract.

It worked when you see an ordinary folder, without a zipper on its icon.


Double-click the zip in Finder. It is extracted into a folder of the same name, next to the zip. Move that folder into your course folder.
Safari extracts zips by itself after downloading, so you may find a folder in Downloads rather than a zip. That folder is what you need.

title: Before the first lab
text:
File extensions
The last part of a file name, after the dot, says what kind of file it is: .csv is a table, .qmd a Quarto document, .zip a packed folder. Windows and macOS hide it by default, which makes ess-news.csv and ess-news.zip look alike. Make them visible:

WindowsmacOS


In File Explorer, open View > Show and tick File name extensions (Windows 11). On Windows 10, open the View tab and tick File name extensions.


In Finder, open Finder > Settings > Advanced and tick Show all filename extensions.



Two traps this prevents:

Renaming without seeing the extension turns data into data.csv.csv, and R cannot find data.csv.
Saving a .csv from Excel. Opening one in Excel to look at it is fine. Saving it is not: on a Dutch or German computer Excel writes semicolons instead of commas and decimal commas instead of points, and it can change dates and long numbers. Look at data in RStudio instead (View(ess), or click the table in the Environment pane).

If double-clicking a .qmd opens the wrong program, open it from RStudio with File > Open File. To make RStudio the default: on Windows, right-click the file > Open with > Choose another app > RStudio, Always; on a Mac, select the file, press Cmd + I, choose RStudio under Open with and click Change All.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Where your files live
Keep one folder for the course, for example Documents/cadc, and extract every lab into it. After two weeks it looks like this:
cadc/
├── setup-check/
├── week01-lab-a/
│   ├── week01-lab-a-part1.qmd
│   ├── week01-lab-a-part2.qmd
│   ├── ess-news.csv
│   └── guns-polls.csv
├── week01-lab-b/
└── week02-lab-a/

Cloud folders. On many laptops Documents and Desktop are synced to OneDrive (Windows) or iCloud Drive (Mac). That is fine, with one setting: synced files can live only in the cloud until you open them, and R cannot always read those. Right-click your course folder and choose Always keep on this device (OneDrive) or Keep Downloaded (iCloud).
Names. File and folder names without spaces and special characters save typing and mistakes: week01_notes.qmd, not Week 1 notes (final!).qmd.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Paths
A path is the address of a file: the route through the folders to get to it. Click through the six steps below; it is the one idea on this page that most “file not found” errors come down to.
Click through, or use the arrow keys. Open full screen
Copying the path of a file:

WindowsmacOS


Select the file in File Explorer and press Ctrl + Shift + C (Windows 11), or hold Shift, right-click the file and choose Copy as path. You get something like:
"C:\Users\sam\Documents\cadc\week01-lab-a\ess-news.csv"
R reads a \ as the start of a special character, so pasting that gives Error: '\U' used without hex digits in character string. Replace every \ with /:
read_csv("C:/Users/sam/Documents/cadc/week01-lab-a/ess-news.csv")


Select the file in Finder and press Option + Cmd + C. Or right-click it, hold Option, and choose Copy … as Pathname. You get something like:
/Users/sam/Documents/cadc/week01-lab-a/ess-news.csv



In the labs you will rarely need a full path, and you should not hand one in: a line with C:/Users/sam/... in it runs on Sam’s laptop and nowhere else. Keep the data next to the .qmd and use the file name alone. A data file in a subfolder is data/ess-news.csv; .. means one folder up.

title: Before the first lab
text:
R and your folders
R looks for files in one folder at a time, the working directory.

In a .qmd file, the working directory is the folder the .qmd is in, both when you run a chunk and when you click Render.
In the console, it is a separate folder, usually your home folder. A line you type in the console therefore looks somewhere else than the same line in a chunk.
To check: getwd() prints the working directory, list.files() the files in it.
Avoid setwd("C:/Users/..."). It works on one computer only, and inside a .qmd it lasts for one chunk. Move the files instead.

Try it once. Open setup-check.qmd, add a chunk at the end (Ctrl + Alt + I, on a Mac Cmd + Option + I), and run:
writeLines("Hello from R", "hello.txt")
Find hello.txt in File Explorer or Finder, and in RStudio’s Files pane at the bottom right. Then type the same line into the console, press Enter, and find out where that copy went (getwd() tells you). Delete both files afterwards.
A shortcut that prevents typos: type read_csv(" and press Tab. RStudio lists the files in the working directory; type the first letters and press Tab again. If the file is not in the list, R will not find it either.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Installing software
What you might see, and what to do.
R asks Do you want to install from sources the packages which need compilation? (Yes/no/cancel). Answer no. The newest version of a package is sometimes not yet prepared (“compiled”) for your system. Yes means your computer has to compile it, which needs extra tools you probably do not have. No gives you the previous, ready-made version, which is fine.
R asks Would you like to use a personal library instead?. Answer yes, and yes again when it offers to create one. Packages then go into a folder of your own.
R warns Rtools is required to build R packages (Windows). Ignore it. You only need Rtools to compile packages, see above.
Error: there is no package called ‘tidytext’. The package is not installed. Run install.packages("tidytext") once.
Error: could not find function “read_csv”. The package is installed but not loaded in this session, or the name has a typo. Run the library(...) line at the top of the file. Installing happens once per computer; library() once per session.
Mac: RStudio is gone after a restart, or there is an RStudio disk in the Finder sidebar. You ran it from the download instead of installing it. Drag RStudio into Applications, then eject the disk.
Mac: the setup check says you have the Intel version of R. Download the installer ending in arm64.pkg from CRAN, install it over the old one, restart RStudio and install the course packages again.
Your R is more than a year old. Install the current version the same way as the first time, then run the package line from step 4 again: packages belong to one R version. RStudio updates itself through Help > Check for Updates.

title: Before the first lab
text:
RStudio in five minutes
RStudio has four panes. Top left is the editor, where your .qmd file is open. Bottom left is the console, where R runs things and prints the results. Top right, Environment lists the objects you have made. Bottom right, Files shows the working directory, and Plots and Help appear there too.
A .qmd file mixes text with grey code chunks. Three ways to run code:

One line: put the cursor on it and press Ctrl + Enter (Cmd + Enter on a Mac). The cursor moves to the next line, so you can step through a chunk.
One chunk: click the green ▶ at its top right.
Everything above: the small grey ▼ next to the ▶ runs all chunks before this one. Use it when R says an object does not exist because you skipped a chunk.

Render runs the whole file from the top in a fresh session and makes a web page of it. If a file renders with an error but worked when you ran it chunk by chunk, it depended on something you did in the console.
What the console is telling you:

> means R is ready.
+ means R is waiting for you to finish a command, usually a missing ) or ". Press Esc to start over.
A small red stop sign at the top right of the console means R is busy. Wait, or press Esc to interrupt it.

When things behave oddly, restart R (Session > Restart R) and run the file again from the top.

title: Before the first lab
text:
When something goes wrong
Read the last line of the error first. It usually names the problem:



R says
What it usually means




object 'ess' not found
The line that makes ess has not run yet in this session, or the name has a typo. Run the chunks above (the grey ▼).


could not find function "..."
The package is not loaded: run the library() line. Or a typo.


'ess-news.csv' does not exist in current working directory
R is looking in another folder than the file is in. See Paths.


there is no package called '...'
Not installed yet. See Installing software.


unexpected symbol, unexpected ')'
A typo: often a missing comma or bracket on that line or the one before.


unexpected input
Often curly quotes, see below.



Curly quotes. Code copied from a PDF, Word or slides often turns " into “ and ”, which R does not accept. Retype the quotes in RStudio, or copy code from the course website with the copy button at the top right of each code box.
Restart and run again. Session > Restart R, then run the file from the top. Many puzzling errors come from leftovers of an earlier attempt.
Asking for help. Say what you ran, what you expected, and paste the error as text, not a photo of your screen. For a screenshot, use Win + Shift + S or Cmd + Shift + 4, then Space. If it is about installing, add the output of the setup check.
